newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army denies killing returning Hutus.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army denies killing returning Hutus.

text.p: Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army on Wednesday denied killing dozens of suspected Hutu rebels who disappeared at a border crossing with war-torn east Zaire.

Refugees, aid workers, diplomats and human rights officials say the army has screened thousands of Hutu refugees forced home to Burundi from east Zaire since fighting erupted two weeks ago, and dozens of people taken away have not been seen since.
They presume they were killed, as dozens of bodies of men, women and children are washing up on the shores of Lake Tanganyika at the south end of the border between Zaire and Burundi.
Burundian army spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi denied any involvement by his troops and attributed the bodies to the anarchy across the frontier.
"There has been no screening and there have been no killings of refugees by the army on Burundian territory," he said. The army has denied any involvement in fighting in Zaire.
Diplomats and human rights officials say the Burundi army co-operated with ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels, who now control eastern Zaire, in weeding out its enemies.

"They (the army) separated the refugees into Rwandans and Burundians about five km (three miles) back from the border and looked for (Hutu rebel) membership cards. On the basis of that they singled people out and executed them," a senior foreign diplomat said, basing his information on reliable contacts.
"But it also seems that they executed the families of the men killed," he said. He declined to be named.
Burundi's three-year-old civil war between the Tutsi-dominated government and Hutu rebels has claimed 150,000 lives.

Burundi's army has been burying corpses of at least 31 men, women and children by Lake Tanganyika. Many had their hands tied behind their backs, suggesting they were executed and thrown into the Rusizi river that flows down the border to the lake.
Local fishermen say they have buried 50 bodies since the conflict erupted and witnesses said on Monday 50 more were unburied on a beach near the east Zairean town of Uvira.
Tens of thousands of other Burundian Hutu refugees have joined Rwandan Hutus in fleeing west and away from the Tutsi rebels and their former homelands.
But around 11,000 Burundian Hutus have arrived at a transit site at Gatumba just inside Burundi after being told to leave Zaire by Banyamulenge rebels who seized the area two weeks ago.
The returnees are being trucked to communes in Cibitoke, Bubanza and Bujumbura provinces despite warnings by aid workers of insecurity in Burundi's interior.
The largest group is to return to Cibitoke, a no-go area for the United Nations and aid agencies, where fighting has increased since the fall of camps north of Uvira.

Burundi's military regime came to power on July 25 in an coup that brought ethnic Tutsi Pierre Buyoya to power. Regional states including Tanzania, Kenya and Zaire imposed sanctions on Burundi six days later.
